content: Inotropes are frequently administered to preterm infants to manage systemic hypotension. Among these, dopamine and dobutamine are the most commonly utilized agents. These two drugs operate through distinct mechanisms of action, which may lead to differing hemodynamic effects. The purpose of this review was to evaluate and compare the efficacy and safety of dopamine and dobutamine in treating systemic hypotension in preterm infants. The review included randomized controlled trials that assessed either the short-term or long-term effects of these treatments. Eligible studies focused on newborns born before 37 weeks of gestation and less than 28 days old. Systemic arterial hypotension was defined according to the criteria used in individual studies. There were no restrictions based on birth weight, gestational age, or the method and duration of inotropic administration. The quality and eligibility of the studies were independently assessed by reviewers. Data extraction was conducted independently by each reviewer, and any discrepancies were resolved through discussion. The outcomes analyzed included neonatal mortality, long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes, radiological evidence of severe neurological injury, short-term hemodynamic changes, and the incidence of adverse effects. The effects of the interventions were quantified using Relative Risk (RR), Risk Difference (RD), or Weighted Mean Difference (WMD), each with a 95% Confidence Interval (CI). Five trials met the inclusion criteria for this review. The analysis revealed no significant difference between dopamine and dobutamine in terms of neonatal mortality (RD 0.02, 95% CI -0.12 to 0.16), the incidence of periventricular leukomalacia (RD -0.08, 95% CI -0.19 to 0.04), or the occurrence of severe periventricular hemorrhage (RD -0.02, 95% CI -0.13 to 0.09). However, dopamine was found to be more effective than dobutamine in managing systemic hypotension, as fewer infants experienced treatment failure with dopamine (RD -0.23, 95% CI -0.34 to -0.13; Number Needed to Treat [NNT] = 4.4, 95% CI 2.9 to 7.7). In one study that reported left ventricular output, dobutamine was associated with a significantly greater increase in this parameter compared to dopamine. There was no significant difference between the two drugs regarding the incidence of tachycardia (RD -0.06, 95% CI -0.25 to 0.14). None of the included studies reported data on adverse long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes. In conclusion, dopamine appears to be more effective than dobutamine for the short-term treatment of systemic hypotension in preterm infants. However, there is no evidence to suggest that either drug affects the incidence of severe periventricular hemorrhage, periventricular leukomalacia, or tachycardia. Importantly, the lack of data on long-term outcomes and safety prevents definitive recommendations regarding the choice of drug for treating hypotension in this population.
